summary: This Best Current Practice document compiles the process for selecting, confirming, and recalling members of the IAB and IESG, and some members of the IAOC, through nominating and recall committees. It was replaced by RFC 8713.

eli5.summary: The groups that guide the internet need new members. This document is the rulebook for how a committee picks them and how they can be removed. It was replaced by RFC 8713.

subtitle: The rulebook for how the IETF picks, confirms and, if needed, removes the people who lead its standards work.

tldr.problem: The IETF needs a fair, repeatable way to fill positions on the IAB, the IESG and some IAOC seats, and a way to remove a sitting member, but the rules were spread over RFC 3777 and several later updates.
tldr.mechanism: A nominating committee of 10 randomly chosen volunteers picks one candidate per open position, a confirming body consents or rejects, and a separate recall committee handles removals with a 3/4 majority vote.
tldr.outcome: It gathered RFC 3777 and its updates into one specification. It was later obsoleted by RFC 8713.

today: RFC 7437 is a Best Current Practice that has been obsoleted by RFC 8713, and it was updated by RFC 8318. It obsoleted RFC 3777, RFC 5078, RFC 5633, RFC 5680 and RFC 6859.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 7437 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 10). It republishes RFC 3777 and the RFCs that updated it as a single specification of how members of the IAB and IESG, and some members of the IAOC, are selected, confirmed and recalled.

Two assumptions carry over: the IRTF and IRSG are not part of this process, and neither is the organization or reorganization of the IESG. Time frames are measured against IETF meetings, assuming three meetings a year, called the First, Second and Third IETF.

The document covers four topics: general rules, selecting the nominating committee, how that committee operates, and member recall.
sections.eli5: This is one big rulebook for choosing the grown-ups who steer the internet's standards. It puts several older rule sheets into one place.

sections.title: General Rules of the Annual Process
sections.content:
The annual process is due to finish within seven months, one month before the Friday of the week before the First IETF. It has three parts: selecting and organizing the nominating committee, choosing candidates, and confirming them. An extra month is set aside before new terms begin, in case any part runs long.

Each year about half of the IESG and IAB positions, and one IAOC position, are reviewed. Confirmed candidates are expected to serve at least a two-year term. The committee does not choose which positions are open and does not confirm its own candidates. Incumbents must tell the committee if they want to be nominated, and there is no term limit.

Mid-term vacancies follow the same rules with changes. The committee has six weeks, a confirming body has two weeks to reject a candidate before consent is assumed, and the new term is either the rest of the old term (if at least a year remains) or the rest plus the next two-year term.

All deliberations about specific nominees and candidates are confidential. Nominees may ask people for feedback but should not encourage public statements of support, and the committee should treat campaigning as unacceptable behavior.
sections.eli5: Every year about half the seats are up for a new pick. The committee suggests people, but someone else has to say yes, and everyone must keep the discussions secret.

sections.title: Building the Nominating Committee
sections.content:
The committee has at least a Chair, 10 voting volunteers, two liaisons and an advisor. The Chair is appointed by the Internet Society President. The IAB and IESG each appoint a liaison from their current members, and the Internet Society Board of Trustees may appoint one. The prior year's Chair serves as an advisor. The Chair, liaisons and advisors do not vote on candidate selection.

To volunteer, a person must have attended at least three of the last five IETF meetings. People serving on the Internet Society Board of Trustees, the IAB, the IESG or the IAOC may not volunteer as voting members. The solicitation must give the community at least 30 days.

The 10 voting members are chosen at random from the pool. The method must use random data whose value is not known until the selection date, must be independently verifiable as fair and unbiased, and must be repeatable. No more than two volunteers with the same primary affiliation may be selected. The members are announced twice, with at least a one week window in which anyone may challenge the result in writing. The second announcement starts the committee's term, which is expected to last 15 months.
sections.eli5: The committee is picked like a raffle, so nobody can rig it. No company can send more than two people, and everyone gets a week to complain if something looks unfair.

sections.title: How the Committee Works
sections.content:
Selecting candidates is due at least two months before the First IETF, and confirmation at least one month before it. The Chair sets milestones and a voting mechanism. A candidate-selection vote needs at least seven voting volunteers present; other votes need at least 75% of members participating. Only voting volunteers vote on candidates.

The Chair announces the open positions and a call for nominees. Anyone in the IETF community may nominate anyone, and self-nomination is allowed. Committee members cannot be considered for positions that their own committee fills, and people recalled in the previous two years are not eligible. A nominee must consent in writing before becoming a candidate, and consent does not imply selection.

The committee then presents a single candidate per open position to the confirming body, with testimony on how the person meets the qualifications. The IAB reviews IESG candidates and the Internet Society Board of Trustees reviews IAB candidates. If a confirming body has no rule of its own, confirming should need at least half of its sitting members. Rejected candidates and nominees must be told before confirmed candidates are announced.

Disputes go to the Internet Society President, who appoints an arbiter. The result is final with no appeal, and the process should finish within two weeks.
sections.eli5: The committee collects names, asks people if they are willing, and picks one person per seat. Another group then says yes or no. If anyone argues about the rules, a referee decides and that is final.

sections.title: Recalling a Sitting Member
sections.content:
At least 20 members of the IETF community who qualify to be nominating committee voters may send a signed petition to the Internet Society President asking for the recall of any sitting IAB, IAOC or IESG member. No more than two signatories may share a primary affiliation, and the Secretariat checks each signer. The petition needs a statement of justification and supporting documents, and it is announced to the community.

The Internet Society President appoints a Recall Committee Chair but must not evaluate the request, because evaluating its leaders is the community's job. The recall committee is built like a nominating committee, except neither the person under investigation nor the petitioners may be members. It must give the member a chance to submit a written statement and consult third parties.

A recall needs a 3/4 majority of the members who vote on the question. If a member is recalled, the seat is filled under the mid-term vacancy rules.
sections.eli5: If enough people think a leader is not doing the job, they can ask for a vote. A special committee looks into it, and three out of four must agree before the leader is removed.

sections.title: Confidentiality as the Security Concern
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is about privacy of people, not about protocols. Investigating candidates can reveal confidential or private information, so everyone who takes part must keep confidential anything not marked as suitable for public release.

When the committee must share such information, the sharing must be minimal and everyone consulted must first commit to the same confidentiality rules as the committee.
sections.eli5: The committee learns private things about people, so everyone promises to keep them secret and to share as little as possible.
